title: The project tech stack
idea: Each tool has one job. Express routes requests, Zod checks input, Drizzle talks to PostgreSQL, and a JWT proves who is calling.
points: Express routes each request through middleware to a handler.
`jsonwebtoken` signs and verifies tokens; `bcryptjs` hashes passwords one way; `nanoid` makes short codes.
Zod checks input against a schema, so bad requests get a clear 400.
Drizzle builds SQL from JavaScript; the `pg` driver sends it to PostgreSQL.

steps.caption: A logged-in client sends `POST /shorten` with a token and a long URL.
Express matches the route and runs its handlers in order.
The auth middleware asks `jsonwebtoken` to verify the token.
The handler asks Zod whether the body holds a valid URL.
Drizzle turns the insert into SQL. The `pg` driver sends it.
PostgreSQL sends the stored row back.
Drizzle hands the row to the handler as a plain JavaScript object.
Express sends the response. `jsonwebtoken` and Zod have no work on the way back.

code.title: Four libraries, one line each
code.caption: A first look at the small libraries. Express, Drizzle and `pg` get their own lessons next.

walk.text: Four imports, one per library. Each is a normal npm package.
`safeParse` checks a value and reports `success`. Lesson 8 uses it on request bodies.
`hash` is slow on purpose. `compare` checks a password against a stored hash.
`sign` packs claims into a token. `sub` holds the user id, and the token expires in one hour.
`verify` checks the signature and expiry, then returns the claims.
`nanoid(7)` makes seven random characters. They differ every run, so only the length prints.

pitfalls: Older tutorials target Express 4 or Zod 3. Check the version before copying code.
Never hard-code real secrets. `demo-secret` and `demo-password` are demo values only.

quiz.why: `compare` hashes the guess with the salt stored inside `hash` and checks for a match. Only the right password matches.

takeaway: Each tool owns one step of a request; know which tool owns which.
